newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid chiefs to give their version of history.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid chiefs to give their version of history.

text.p: General Magnus Malan, security chief in the final decade of apartheid, has stepped forward to defend the way his men enforced the system that destroyed the lives of countless South Africans of all races.

Malan, former armed forces chief and defence minister, volunteered on Wednesday to testify next month to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission which is trying to uncover the crimes and human rights abuses of the apartheid era.
But Malan, second only to former president P.W. Botha as the most senior surviving member of the security apparatus of the 1980s, is not planning to say he is sorry or apply for amnesty.

"I have decided to (testify) because it appears that there is a total lack of military expertise in the truth commission when it comes to assessing the past actions of the South African Defence Force," Malan said in a statement.
"Blatant, untrue and unfair accusations are being made regarding the former SADF in an apparent vendetta...I am not prepared to permit these incorrect perceptions to go unchallenged," he said.

Malan, who has said there is nothing which he needs to confess, decided to cooperate with Archbishop Desmond Tutu's commission after discussions with Botha, the president he served for most of the 1980s.

Botha apparently asked Malan to testify after a meeting last year between the former president and Tutu, who urged Botha to help the commission in its aim of reconciling South Africans by pulling all the apartheid skeletons out of the closet. Botha agreed to intercede with the ministers who served under him.

Political analysts said Botha, Malan and their political colleagues could have been persuaded to give their side of the apartheid story to be recorded by the truth commission ahead of elections looming in 1999.

"The final report of the truth commission is going to become part of the election... nothing stays outside the political arena," said Jannie Gagiano, a political scientist at the University of Stellenbosch.
"People are going to stand on platforms and pull out that report as if it was given to humanity by God, revealing history to us," he said.
Gagiano said the National Party, which ruled from 1948 to 1994 and is now in opposition to the African National Congress, had no sense that it had been criminally wrong in applying apartheid.

"They just feel 'it was hard ball and so on, but that was the way the situation required us to act, and although some of us went overboard, much of what was done was in accordance with what was required'," he said.

Political analysts said Malan was unlikely to have been motivated by fear that he could be implicated in crimes or human rights abuses by the testimony of subordinates who have told the commission they were acting on orders from above.

Malan went on trial for murder last year but was acquitted when the prosecution failed to make charges stick that the defence force was directly linked to an attack on suspected ANC sympathisers by the rival Inkatha Freedom Party.

The analysts said Malan would try to steer his testimony to the truth commission away from the messy details of hit squads and extra-judicial killings, giving instead the broad picture of the fight against Soviet expansion in southern Africa.

Tutu and his deputy chairman, Alex Boraine, have described Malan's decision to testify as a breakthrough for the commission, partly because it could pave the way for many of the soldiers who served under him to come forward with information or applications for amnesty.
The deadline for amnesty applications has been extended to May 10.
